entities.name: Antistius Sosianus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Antistius Sosianus was a Roman aristocrat whose career in the mid-1st century CE became a stark illustration of the perils of political dissent under the Julio-Claudian and Flavian emperors, particularly Nero and Vespasian. Serving as plebeian tribune in AD 56 and praetor in 62, Sosianus's public life was repeatedly disrupted by charges of *maiestas*, or treason, a legal instrument frequently wielded by emperors to suppress perceived threats or critics within the senatorial elite. His repeated exiles, first under Nero and again under Vespasian, underscore the volatile power dynamics between the Roman Senate and the imperial household, reflecting a period when freedom of speech for senators was increasingly curtailed, even as the empire outwardly projected stability. His story thus offers a micro-history of the broader political tensions that defined the early Roman Empire.

Sosianus's initial downfall occurred in AD 62, following his praetorship, when he was accused by Eprius Marcellus of reciting satirical verses about Emperor Nero at a large banquet. This charge of *maiestas* led to his first exile to an unnamed island, a common punishment for political offenses, signaling the emperor's intolerance for any public criticism. Despite being recalled by Nero in AD 66, perhaps as part of a general amnesty or a shift in imperial policy, Sosianus's troubles were far from over. After Nero's suicide in 68 and the tumultuous Year of the Four Emperors, Sosianus was again exiled in AD 70 by Vespasian, who specifically cited the same *maiestas* charges from 62. This second banishment suggests that the original accusations were seen as legitimate grievances by subsequent emperors, or that Sosianus continued to engage in activities deemed subversive.
